sections.html: The pumpkinseed (Lepomis gibbosus) is one of the most beautiful coldwater fishes and has very interesting behaviour. In its natural habitat it grows up to 25 cm.
It is wise to buy small individuals (4-5 cm), as their adaptability is high and they easily adapt to life in the new environment.

The species originates from central parts of the North American continent. The continental climate (hot summers, cold winters) makes the pumpkinseed a hardy fish, so it was transferred by humans to many regions as a food fish. It was first brought to Europe around 1880. Since then it has become a native fish in Europe but has not been able to settle over the whole continent.
The garden pond for pumpkinseeds should contain shallow parts with fine sand. Good growth of submerged plants is also important for the fish. Clear and clean water is preferred.
Pumpkinseeds are small predators which feed on insect larvae, amphibian larvae, small fish and so on. They can be fed easily with frozen bloodworm, but will almost always refuse dried food.
The males defend territories where they take care of the brood until the fry swims free.
Males become bigger than the females and are more colourful.
Pair-binding is not known in the species; the male will readily mate with any female that comes around. The males defend territories where they take care of the brood until the fry swims free.

Nowadays the pumpkinseed is blamed as an unwanted and useless species in Europe. In Europe it usually grows only to 5-10 cm: predators that feed on it in North America are missing, which leads to mass reproduction and dwarfed fish. The perch (Perca fluviatilis) also becomes dwarfed where predators are missing. In aquaria the fish can become much older than in nature and, as it grows its whole life, can reach a considerable size. In the garden pond it usually stays small (around 15 cm). With age its adaptability to environmental change lessens, so most pumpkinseeds die at around 5 years due to weather changes or similar.
